note: Summaries are written by Claude from each paper's abstract. Items marked 'title only' had no abstract available — open the paper before relying on them. This run could not reach the OpenAlex API, so it used web search, the Physics of Fluids current-issue feed and arXiv instead; coverage of JCP, JFM and IJMF is thinner than usual.

items.title: Correcting a capillary-number sign pitfall in Kistler dynamic contact-angle modeling
items.authors: Authors not listed in the journal feed

summary.problem: The common Kistler dynamic contact-angle implementation uses the magnitude of the capillary number, so it loses the sign that distinguishes advancing from receding contact lines.
summary.method: The authors keep the sign in a modified formulation and test both versions in volume-of-fluid simulations of droplet impact and bubble coalescence.
summary.result: The magnitude-based model mispredicts droplet recoil and suppresses bubble detachment, while the corrected model captures both.

items.why: Directly relevant to the contact angle on a moving solid in your proposal: during water entry the contact line on the sphere both advances and recedes, so check whether your Kistler/Cox–Voinov implementation keeps the sign of Ca.

items.title: A Data-Free Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Level-Set Interface Advection

summary.problem: Neural operators for moving interfaces usually need training data from the very solver they replace, and field-norm error metrics miss how far the interface has actually moved.
summary.method: A spacetime Fourier neural operator maps an initial interface to its whole trajectory, trained only on the transport residual plus an eikonal term, with the initial condition built in by construction.
summary.result: On a reversed vortex it reaches about 1.6% relative L2 error versus 0.37% for a supervised baseline (4.4 times worse), but on solid-body rotation it conserves enclosed area 2.7 times better.

items.why: A useful contrast for PLIC-Net: it argues for interface-displacement and area-conservation metrics rather than field norms, which is the same point you would make about volume conservation in learned VOF reconstruction.

items.title: SUMNO: Spatially Unrolled Multigrid Neural Operator for Fluid Flow Surrogates
items.authors: Y. Hu, N. Deng, C. Shao

summary.problem: U-shaped neural surrogates borrow the multigrid layout but their inner parts follow generic vision designs, and accurate prediction of complex flows is still hard.
summary.method: The authors turn a multigrid V-cycle into a feed-forward network with parameter-free restriction/prolongation, additive skips, convolutions on fine grids and shifted-window attention on the coarsest grid.
summary.result: Across four flow benchmarks it ranks first in 5 of 7 settings, cuts 10-step rollout error by about 30% versus the best baseline, and uses only 9.4 million parameters against baselines over 130 million.

items.why: Connects your Poisson condition-number note to the ML thread: a network built to mimic a V-cycle is a natural candidate for a learned preconditioner or initial guess for the variable-density pressure solve.

items.title: DynaSolver: A Neural Operator for Autoregressive 4D Flow Prediction with Dynamic Boundaries
items.authors: R. Qian, S. Dai, M. Lin et al.

summary.problem: Most neural CFD surrogates assume a fixed geometry, so they cannot predict unsteady flow around continuously moving boundaries.
summary.method: DynaSolver conditions on boundary motion and flow history through compact physical tokens and is trained with replay-augmented parallel training on its own rollouts.
summary.result: The abstract gives no numbers but reports the best full-rollout accuracy on the RoboCFD-4D benchmark, with the advantage growing over longer rollouts.

items.why: Single-phase, but it tackles the same 'solid moving without remeshing' requirement from the learning side; worth a sentence in the ML outlook of your review.

items.title: Axisymmetric numerical simulation of a conducting drop impact onto a deep pool under a vertical uniform magnetic field: Capillary wave propagation on the main drop side
items.authors: Authors not listed in the journal feed

summary.problem: The surface-wave patterns produced when a liquid-metal drop hits a deep pool under a vertical magnetic field are not well classified.
summary.method: Axisymmetric VOF simulations with adaptive mesh refinement over a wide range of Reynolds and Weber numbers.
summary.result: Phase diagrams separate single-wave, multi-wave and small-eddy regimes, and a stronger magnetic field shifts the regime boundaries.

items.why: Impact onto a deep pool with crater and capillary waves is the liquid analogue of your water-entry cavity cases; their AMR/VOF regime maps are a good template for presenting parameter sweeps.

items.title: Effect of superhydrophobic obstacles on the impact dynamics of a shear-thinning droplet
items.authors: Authors not listed in the journal feed

summary.problem: How the curvature of a superhydrophobic obstacle changes the impact of a shear-thinning droplet.
summary.method: Numerical simulations of droplets hitting cube, cylinder and hemisphere obstacles, analysed with deformation, anisotropy, energy budgets and curvature indices.
summary.result: Contact persists at low Weber number, detachment is intermittent at intermediate values and rapid at high values; the hemisphere gives the largest kinetic-energy gain during retraction.

items.why: Wetting on curved solids is topic 3 of your list; check how they impose the contact angle on non-grid-aligned curved walls, the same problem as on your sphere.

items.title: Coalescence mechanisms of micro- and nanobubbles: Insights from in situ imaging and multiphysics modeling
items.authors: Authors not listed in the journal feed

summary.problem: Nanobubble coalescence, which can turn stable nanobubbles into microbubbles, is poorly understood.
summary.method: High-resolution in situ imaging with machine-learning image recognition, combined with VOF simulations.
summary.result: Nanobubbles coalesce much more slowly than microbubbles, and VOF simulations match the observed film drainage better than no-slip models.

items.why: Thin-film drainage between interfaces is the same physics as the air film in your solver; their comparison of slip assumptions bears on your sub-cell gas-layer rule.

items.title: EDP-PI-DOSnet: An Energy Dissipation Preserving Neural Solver for Two-Phase Flow Problems

summary.method: From the title: a physics-informed neural solver for two-phase flow designed to preserve the energy-dissipation law.
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: If it targets phase-field/two-phase PDEs with a structure-preserving loss, it is a direct comparison point for PINN-with-VOF work; read before citing.

items.title: Accelerating matrix-free fast diagonalization and preconditioned linear solvers for high-order finite element discretized elliptic problems on distributed GPUs

summary.method: From the title: GPU-accelerated matrix-free fast-diagonalization preconditioners for high-order finite-element elliptic (Poisson-type) problems.
summary.result: Open the paper to see results.

items.why: Relevant to the pressure-solve cost discussion in your Poisson note and as a classical baseline for the quantum solver study; check whether it handles variable coefficients.

items.title: Wall-mobility effects on evaporation feedback in a droplet model inspired by surface acoustic waves
items.authors: Authors not listed in the journal feed

summary.problem: Ignoring evaporation in acoustically deformed droplets causes an interface error that depends on how easily liquid slides along the wall.
summary.method: A verified axisymmetric long-wave model with evaporation, thermocapillarity, precursor films and wall slip (no-slip, Navier and threshold slip).
summary.result: Mobile walls (Navier and threshold slip) shift the evaporation-error crossing more under acoustic forcing than no-slip walls.

items.why: Shows quantitatively how the slip model at the contact line changes outcomes, a point to raise when you discuss mesh dependence and slip length in contact-line models.

items.title: Dynamic wetting characteristics of nanoscale water films on regular textured surfaces under periodic vibration
items.authors: Authors not listed in the journal feed

summary.problem: How vibration amplitude and period control the wetting of nanoscale water films on grooved surfaces.
summary.method: Molecular dynamics with free-energy analysis, molecular velocity statistics and phase diagrams.
summary.result: Five wetting outcomes are found, and the transition boundary follows a scaling law whose constant depends on film thickness, groove aspect ratio and Young's contact angle.

items.why: Molecular-scale background for contact-angle hysteresis and pinning on textured, moving surfaces; useful for the physics section of the review rather than the methods.

items.title: Two-phase flow simulations of surface waves and turbulence underneath
items.authors: Authors not listed in the journal feed

summary.problem: How surface waves interact with countercurrent turbulence beneath the air-water interface.
summary.method: A hybrid scale-resolving method that resolves both air and water, with synthetic turbulence generation.
summary.result: Waves amplify near-surface streamwise enstrophy by up to 6 times, and pressure drag scales with the square of wave slope.

items.why: Background for turbulence near a free surface; lower priority, but a reference if your water-entry cases reach turbulent cavity closure.
